texts: Comprehensive cover: Cover that pays to repair or replace my own car if I crash it, as well as the other person's damage
Comprehensive cover: The most complete type of car policy, including theft, fire and accidental damage
Comprehensive cover: Our highest level of motor cover, protecting your own car as well as other people's property.
Comprehensive cover: I spilled or dropped something; knocked something over and broke it
What's covered (Comprehensive cover): Accidental damage, fire, theft and malicious damage to your vehicle, plus your liability to third parties under the Road Traffic Act.
What's not covered (Comprehensive cover): Wear and tear, mechanical breakdown, unlicensed drivers and any loss caused by driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs.
Costs and excess (Comprehensive cover): You pay the compulsory and any voluntary excess on each claim; the premium depends on your rating factors at quote or renewal.
How to claim (Comprehensive cover): Report the incident through My Insura or our motor claims line; we appoint an approved repairer and agree the repair estimate.
Third party, fire and theft: A cheaper policy that does not pay to fix my car if I cause a crash but does cover it being stolen or burnt
Third party, fire and theft: Insurance covering other people's property and my car only if it is stolen or set on fire
Third party, fire and theft: A middle level of cover that insures damage you cause to others plus loss of your car through fire or theft.
Third party, fire and theft: TPFT
Third party, fire and theft: third party fire theft
Third party, fire and theft: I spilled or dropped something; knocked something over and broke it
What's covered (Third party, fire and theft): Liability for injury and damage to others, and loss of or damage to your car caused by fire, theft or attempted theft.
What's not covered (Third party, fire and theft): Accidental damage to your own car where you are at fault, and damage from vandalism that is not linked to an attempted theft.
Costs and excess (Third party, fire and theft): Premiums are usually lower than comprehensive; excesses apply to fire and theft claims and are shown on your policy schedule.
How to claim (Third party, fire and theft): Report theft to the police first and give us the crime reference number before we can open a theft claim.
Third party only: The bare minimum insurance I need to drive legally, paying only for harm I cause to other people
Third party only: A policy that never pays for my own car, only for the other driver's costs
Third party only: The minimum cover required by law, protecting you against claims from other people but not paying for your own car.
Third party only: legal minimum cover
Third party only: minimum car insurance
What's covered (Third party only): Your legal liability for injury to other people and damage to their vehicles or property, up to the limits in your policy.
What's not covered (Third party only): Any loss of or damage to your own vehicle, including theft, fire and damage you cause yourself.
Costs and excess (Third party only): The lowest-priced level of cover, though some drivers find comprehensive is similar in price after rating factors are applied.
How to claim (Third party only): Tell us promptly about any incident involving another party and do not admit liability or agree a settlement without us.
Excesses explained: The part of any repair bill that comes out of my own pocket when I make a claim
Excesses explained: What I pay first when something goes wrong, and how choosing a higher amount changes my price
Excesses explained: The compulsory and voluntary excess are the amounts you pay towards a claim before we pay the rest.
Excesses explained: how much I pay towards a claim
What is an excess (Excesses explained): The amount you contribute to a claim; it is made up of a compulsory excess set by us and any voluntary excess you choose.
Choosing a voluntary excess (Excesses explained): A higher voluntary excess usually lowers your premium but means paying more if you claim, so pick an amount you could afford.
Young and inexperienced driver excess (Excesses explained): An additional compulsory excess may apply where the driver is under 25 or has held a licence for less than a year.
When the excess is not charged (Excesses explained): Windscreen repair, and claims where we recover all our costs from the at-fault party, may carry no excess in the end.
Breakdown cover: Help if my car stops working on the road, including towing it to a garage
Breakdown cover: Optional extra that gets a mechanic to me when the car will not start
Breakdown cover: My car has stopped working and will not start while I am out
Breakdown cover: An optional add-on that sends a patrol or recovery vehicle if your car breaks down or will not start.
What's covered (Breakdown cover): Roadside repair, recovery to a local garage or home and onward travel, depending on the level of breakdown cover chosen.
Levels of breakdown cover (Breakdown cover): Roadside only, national recovery and national recovery with at-home start are offered; each adds distance and call-out benefits.
What's not covered (Breakdown cover): Repairs after the roadside visit, parts, fuel, and breakdowns within the first 24 hours of the policy starting.
How to use your cover (Breakdown cover): Call the breakdown line on your card with your policy number and exact location; keep the vehicle somewhere safe while you wait.
Courtesy car: A loan car while mine is in the garage after a crash
Courtesy car: Getting around while my car is being fixed following an insured incident
Courtesy car: An optional add-on providing a small replacement vehicle while your car is being repaired after a claim.
Courtesy car: hire car after accident
What's covered (Courtesy car): A small hatchback for as long as an approved repairer has your car after a valid claim, subject to availability.
What's not covered (Courtesy car): Cars lent while a claim is investigated, after theft where the vehicle is a total loss, or for non-approved repairers.
Conditions of use (Courtesy car): The courtesy car driver must be named, hold a full licence and meet the hire company's age and deposit requirements.
Adding or removing the courtesy car (Courtesy car): Change this cover at any time through My Insura; the premium adjusts from the date of the change.
Motor legal expenses: Help paying a solicitor to get back money I lost in a crash that was not my fault
Motor legal expenses: Support taking another driver to court or negotiating compensation for my injuries
Motor legal expenses: An optional add-on helping with legal costs to pursue uninsured losses after an accident that was not your fault.
Motor legal expenses: uninsured loss recovery
What's covered (Motor legal expenses): Legal costs of pursuing claims for uninsured losses and personal injury, and defence of certain motoring prosecutions, up to the policy limit.
What's not covered (Motor legal expenses): Disputes with us, claims you cause, and cases our panel solicitors assess as having less than a reasonable chance of success.
The legal helpline (Motor legal expenses): A 24-hour helpline offers initial advice on motor-related legal problems; it gives general information rather than representing you.
How to make a legal expenses claim (Motor legal expenses): Contact us before instructing a solicitor so that our panel can accept the case and agree costs in advance.
Windscreen cover: A stone chipped my glass, so I want it fixed without losing my discount
Windscreen cover: Fixing or replacing a cracked car window or windscreen
Windscreen cover: Cover for repair or replacement of damaged windscreens and windows, which usually carries a reduced excess.
Windscreen cover: years without claiming; my NCD
What's covered (Windscreen cover): Repair or replacement of the windscreen, side and rear windows, including fitting and the cost of replacement seals.
Repair or replace (Windscreen cover): Chips smaller than a two-pence coin outside the driver's line of sight are normally repaired rather than replaced.
Excess and no-claims discount (Windscreen cover): A glass claim carries a lower excess and, with comprehensive cover, does not usually affect your no-claims discount.
How to claim (Windscreen cover): Book through our glass partner using My Insura or the claims line; repair can often happen at home or work.
Named drivers: Letting my partner or a friend drive my car legally
Named drivers: Putting another person on my policy so they are covered behind the wheel
Named drivers: Adding other people to your policy so they can drive your car with your insurance in place.
Named drivers: add my husband or wife to the insurance
Named drivers: let my partner drive my car
Named drivers: years without claiming; my NCD
Who can be named (Named drivers): Any licensed driver aged 17 or over, though their age, history and claims record can change your premium.
Adding or removing a named driver (Named drivers): Use My Insura to add or remove a driver; changes take effect on the date you choose and may adjust your price.
Driving other cars (Named drivers): Some policies include limited third-party cover for named drivers in cars they do not own; check your policy wording.

Named driver and no-claims discount (Named drivers): A named driver does not earn their own no-claims discount unless the policyholder is the main driver, and they should not be misrepresented as the main driver.
Young and newly qualified drivers: Insurance for my teenager who has just passed their driving test
Young and newly qualified drivers: Cover options for someone who is learning to drive or only recently qualified
Young and newly qualified drivers: How cover works for drivers under 25 or who passed their test in the last two years.
Young and newly qualified drivers: learner driver
Young and newly qualified drivers: new driver
Young and newly qualified drivers: under 25 car insurance
Young and newly qualified drivers: years without claiming; my NCD
Why young drivers pay more (Young and newly qualified drivers): Insurers rate drivers under 25 and those new to driving as higher risk, which increases premiums and excesses.
Learner driver cover (Young and newly qualified drivers): Short-term cover lets a learner practise in a family car for days or weeks without affecting the main policyholder's no-claims discount.
Pass Plus and driver training (Young and newly qualified drivers): Completing an approved course such as Pass Plus may qualify for a discount on some policies.
Ways to reduce the cost (Young and newly qualified drivers): Choosing a smaller engine, a higher voluntary excess, a telematics policy or being named on a parent's policy can help.
Business use and commuting: Using my own car for my job and making sure I am insured for it
Business use and commuting: Whether driving to work or between customers is covered by my normal policy
Business use and commuting: What counts as social, commuting or business use of your car and how this affects cover and price.
Business use and commuting: class 1 business use
Business use and commuting: commuting cover
Business use and commuting: driving for work
Social, domestic and pleasure (Business use and commuting): Covers everyday personal use but not travel to a regular place of work or any use connected with a business.
Commuting (Business use and commuting): Add commuting if you drive to a fixed workplace; it is a higher class of use, so you will need to tell us.
Business use (Business use and commuting): Use for visits to clients or carrying tools is business use; carrying goods or passengers for hire needs specialist cover.
Telling us about a change (Business use and commuting): Tell us as soon as your use changes; failing to do so could lead to a claim being reduced or declined.
Driving abroad: Taking my car on a trip to France or Spain and staying insured
Driving abroad: Whether my UK policy pays out if I have an accident in another country
Driving abroad: Cover for taking your car to other countries, including green card requirements and breakdown abroad.
Driving abroad: taking my car to europe
Minimum cover abroad (Driving abroad): Most policies give at least the legal minimum cover in other countries for up to 90 days a year, though not full comprehensive cover.
Extending to comprehensive abroad (Driving abroad): Ask us to extend to full cover for a trip; this may be free or charged, depending on destination and length.
Documents to carry (Driving abroad): Take your driving licence, vehicle registration document and a green card or insurance certificate where one is requested.
If you break down or crash abroad (Driving abroad): Contact us and any breakdown provider quickly; keep receipts and police reports to support your claim.
How your no-claims discount works: Paying less each year because I have not crashed
How your no-claims discount works: How many years without claiming gets me the biggest saving
How your no-claims discount works: The discount you earn for each claim-free year, and what happens to it if you make a claim.
How your no-claims discount works: NCD
How your no-claims discount works: no claims bonus
How your no-claims discount works: no claims discount
How your no-claims discount works: years without claiming; my NCD
Earning your discount (How your no-claims discount works): You earn one year for each full year you hold a policy without a claim where we pay out and cannot recover our costs.
What happens when you claim (How your no-claims discount works): A claim you are at fault for normally reduces your discount by two years, or sets it back to a lower step.
Using a company car or other vehicle (How your no-claims discount works): Time driving another car as a named driver or on a company vehicle may sometimes count, if you hold written proof.
Discount if you stop driving (How your no-claims discount works): Your discount is usually valid for two years after a policy ends, so you can restart cover without losing it.
Proof of your no-claims discount: A letter I can show my new insurer to prove I have not made a claim
Proof of your no-claims discount: Getting evidence of my years without claiming when I switch companies
Proof of your no-claims discount: How to get a letter or document showing how many years of claim-free driving you have earned.
Proof of your no-claims discount: NCD proof
Proof of your no-claims discount: no claims letter
Proof of your no-claims discount: no claims certificate
Proof of your no-claims discount: years without claiming; my NCD
Where to find your proof (Proof of your no-claims discount): Download your current proof from the Documents area of My Insura at any time during the policy.
Proof after you cancel (Proof of your no-claims discount): When a policy ends we issue a final proof showing the years earned, normally within five working days.
Information on the letter (Proof of your no-claims discount): It shows the policyholder, the number of years, the dates of cover and whether the discount is protected.
If your proof is lost or wrong (Proof of your no-claims discount): Ask us for a replacement through secure messages; we will reissue the document at no charge.
Protected no-claims discount: Paying extra so one small accident does not wipe out my safe-driving discount
Protected no-claims discount: An optional extra to keep my claim-free savings after a claim
Protected no-claims discount: An add-on that lets you make a limited number of claims without losing your discount.
Protected no-claims discount: protect my no claims
Protected no-claims discount: no claims protection
Protected no-claims discount: years without claiming; my NCD
What protection does (Protected no-claims discount): You can make up to two at-fault claims in three years without your discount step falling, though your premium may still rise.
Cost of protection (Protected no-claims discount): Pricing depends on how many years of discount you hold; it is shown separately at quote and renewal.
When it does not apply (Protected no-claims discount): Protection may not apply to a claim after a conviction for a serious driving offence or a lapse in cover.
Adding or removing protection (Protected no-claims discount): Change this on My Insura; you will be asked to confirm that you have no claims you have not told us about.
Black box and app-based insurance: A policy that watches my driving through an app so careful drivers pay less
Black box and app-based insurance: A fitted box in the car that records speed and braking to set my price
Black box and app-based insurance: Insurance where a device or smartphone app measures how you drive and rewards safer habits with a lower price.
Black box and app-based insurance: telematics
Black box and app-based insurance: black box insurance
Black box and app-based insurance: driving score app
Black box and app-based insurance: pay how you drive
How telematics works (Black box and app-based insurance): A small device or our app records speed, braking, cornering, time of day and mileage, and scores each journey.
Your driving score (Black box and app-based insurance): Scores are reviewed monthly; a consistently good score earns a premium reduction at renewal.
Mileage and night driving (Black box and app-based insurance): Policies set a mileage limit, and regular driving between midnight and 5am may reduce your score.
Fitting, returning and privacy (Black box and app-based insurance): A fitter installs the box free; return it within 30 days if you cancel; data is kept as described in our privacy notice.
Buildings insurance: Insurance for the bricks and roof of the house I own
Buildings insurance: Protecting the structure of my property against fire, storm and subsidence
Buildings insurance: Cover for the structure of your home: walls, roof, floors, fixed fittings and outbuildings.
Buildings insurance: insure the house itself
What's covered (Buildings insurance): Damage to walls, roof, floors, windows, fixed baths and kitchens, plus garages and fences, from insured causes such as fire and storm.
What's not covered (Buildings insurance): Wear and tear, gradual deterioration, faulty workmanship and damage you cause by neglecting maintenance.
Rebuild cost and sum insured (Buildings insurance): Your sum insured should equal the cost of rebuilding the property, not its market value.
Mortgage lender requirements (Buildings insurance): Most lenders require buildings cover from completion; send them your schedule from My Insura.
Contents insurance: Insurance for my sofa, TV and clothes if they are stolen or ruined
Contents insurance: Protecting the things I own in my flat or house
Contents insurance: Cover for belongings inside your home such as furniture, electronics, clothes and carpets.
Contents insurance: jewellery such as a ring or watch; expensive items I take out with me; adding an engagement ring
What's covered (Contents insurance): Furniture, appliances, clothing, jewellery up to single-item limits, and items stored in a locked garage or shed.
What's not covered (Contents insurance): Money above the cash limit, items left unattended in gardens, and loss without evidence of ownership.
Calculating your sum insured (Contents insurance): Add up replacement-as-new values room by room; underinsuring may reduce any claim payment.
Home contents away from home (Contents insurance): Items taken outside the home have limited cover unless you add personal possessions cover.
Buildings and contents together: One policy for both my house and everything in it
Buildings and contents together: Insuring the property and my belongings together to save money
Buildings and contents together: A single policy covering both the building and what is inside it, often at a lower combined price.
Buildings and contents together: combined home insurance
Buildings and contents together: buildings and contents policy
Benefits of combining (Buildings and contents together): One renewal date, one excess to pay in many cases, and a combined discount compared with buying separately.
When to choose separate policies (Buildings and contents together): Tenants only need contents; owners with a leasehold flat may find the freeholder already insures the structure.
Excess on a combined claim (Buildings and contents together): A single claim affecting both building and contents normally carries only one excess.
Switching to combined cover (Buildings and contents together): Add buildings or contents through My Insura; your new schedule shows the combined sums insured.
Escape of water: A pipe burst and water came through the ceiling
Escape of water: Water from a washing machine or tank that has ruined the floor and walls
Escape of water: Cover for damage from water that escapes from pipes, tanks or appliances.
Escape of water: flood from inside
Escape of water: a burst pipe; water leaking through the ceiling
What's covered (Escape of water): Sudden damage from escaping water from plumbing, heating systems, washing machines and dishwashers, including drying-out costs.
What's not covered (Escape of water): The cost of repairing the burst pipe itself, gradual leaks, and flooding from rivers or the sea.
What to do straight away (Escape of water): Turn off the water at the stopcock, switch off electricity if safe, photograph damage and call us.
Trace and access (Escape of water): We pay reasonable costs to find the leak and make good the walls or floors opened up.
Accidental damage: I put my foot through a laptop or knocked over a vase and want it replaced
Accidental damage: Cover for sudden mishaps such as a drill through a pipe or a cracked TV screen
Accidental damage: Optional protection for sudden, unexpected damage to your home or belongings that is not covered elsewhere.
Accidental damage: I spilled or dropped something; knocked something over and broke it
What's covered (Accidental damage): Sudden physical damage to buildings or contents caused by an accident, such as breaking a window or damaging a television.
What's not covered (Accidental damage): Damage by pets, wear and tear, cosmetic scratches, and breakage while an item is being repaired or cleaned.
Buildings and contents versions (Accidental damage): Accidental damage can be added to buildings, contents or both, with separate excesses.
Claiming (Accidental damage): Describe how the damage happened; we may ask for photos and a repair quote.
Theft and burglary: Someone broke in and took my laptop and jewellery
Theft and burglary: A thief damaged my door lock getting into the house
Theft and burglary: Cover for items stolen from your home and damage caused by thieves breaking in.
What's covered (Theft and burglary): Stolen contents and damage to doors, windows and locks caused by forced entry or an attempt to break in.
Security conditions (Theft and burglary): Approved locks on external doors and windows may be a condition; check your schedule for the requirements.
What's not covered (Theft and burglary): Theft by someone you let in, or where no evidence of forced entry exists and your policy requires it.
What to do after a break-in (Theft and burglary): Report to the police, get a crime reference number and ring our claims line promptly.
Storm, flood and weather: A storm took tiles off my roof and rain came in
Storm, flood and weather: Heavy rain flooded my ground floor from the river
Storm, flood and weather: Cover for damage to your home from storms, flooding, snow and heavy rainfall.
Storm, flood and weather: storm damage
Storm, flood and weather: flood damage
Storm, flood and weather: roof blown off
Storm, flood and weather: weather damage
Storm, flood and weather: struggling to afford essentials; help buying school uniforms or food; money is tight
What's covered (Storm, flood and weather): Damage caused by storm winds, rising water from rivers or rainfall, and the weight of snow, including fences and gates in some cases.
What's not covered (Storm, flood and weather): Damage to gates, hedges and fences from storms unless your cover specifically includes them; gradual seepage.
Flood-risk areas (Storm, flood and weather): We may apply a higher excess or exclusions in high-risk areas; Flood Re can help with cover for homes built before 2009.
Alternative accommodation (Storm, flood and weather): If you cannot live at home after an insured loss, we pay reasonable rent and living costs.
Subsidence, heave and landslip: Cracks have appeared in my walls and I think the ground is moving
Subsidence, heave and landslip: My extension is sinking away from the main house
Subsidence, heave and landslip: Cover for movement of the ground beneath your home that damages the building.
Subsidence, heave and landslip: cracks in walls
Subsidence, heave and landslip: sinking house
Subsidence, heave and landslip: ground movement
Subsidence, heave and landslip: keep my number when I switch; move my number to another network
What's covered (Subsidence, heave and landslip): Damage to the building caused by the ground sinking, rising or sliding, usually under buildings insurance.
What's not covered (Subsidence, heave and landslip): Damage from poor construction, settling of new buildings and damage to boundary walls unless the main property is damaged.
Higher excess (Subsidence, heave and landslip): A subsidence excess usually applies, commonly £1,000, in addition to the standard compulsory excess.
Reporting cracks (Subsidence, heave and landslip): Tell us as soon as you see cracks; we may arrange monitoring and a structural survey.
Frozen pipes and heating: The pipes froze while we were away and burst
Frozen pipes and heating: Whether leaving the heating off could affect my claim
Frozen pipes and heating: Cover for damage caused when pipes freeze and burst, and conditions about keeping your home heated.
Frozen pipes and heating: frozen pipe
Frozen pipes and heating: burst pipe in winter
Frozen pipes and heating: empty property in winter
What's covered (Frozen pipes and heating): Damage from frozen pipes or tanks bursting, subject to the conditions around heating while the property is unoccupied.
Unoccupancy conditions (Frozen pipes and heating): If the home is empty for more than 30 days, cover for frozen pipes and some other perils may be restricted.
Preventing freezing (Frozen pipes and heating): Keep the heating on low, drain down the system if leaving for a long time and know where the stopcock is.
How to claim (Frozen pipes and heating): Contact us as soon as it is safe, with photographs and a plumber's report if available.
Alternative accommodation: The house is unlivable and we need somewhere to stay while it is repaired
Alternative accommodation: Paying for a rental or hotel after a fire or flood
Alternative accommodation: Help with living costs if you cannot stay in your home after an insured incident.
Alternative accommodation: hotel after fire or flood
Alternative accommodation: struggling to afford essentials; help buying school uniforms or food; money is tight
What's covered (Alternative accommodation): Reasonable rent, hotel costs and extra living expenses while your home is uninhabitable after an insured event.
Limits and time (Alternative accommodation): Cover is usually capped at a percentage of the buildings sum insured or a set number of months.
Receipts and evidence (Alternative accommodation): Keep receipts for accommodation and meals; we only pay costs above your normal living expenses.
Landlord's rent loss (Alternative accommodation): Landlord policies can pay lost rent while the property is being repaired, if rental income cover is included.
Personal possessions outside the home: My phone was taken from my bag in a cafe
Personal possessions outside the home: Extra protection for my laptop and bike when I leave the house
Personal possessions outside the home: Optional cover for valuables such as phones, cameras and bikes when you take them out.
Personal possessions outside the home: gadget cover
Personal possessions outside the home: bicycle cover
Personal possessions outside the home: items away from home
Personal possessions outside the home: jewellery such as a ring or watch; expensive items I take out with me; adding an engagement ring
What's covered (Personal possessions outside the home): Named items you carry away from home, such as mobile phones, cameras, laptops and cycles, for loss, theft or damage.
Items over the single-item limit (Personal possessions outside the home): Valuables above the limit must be listed individually with a description and value.
Cycling cover (Personal possessions outside the home): Cycles are covered when locked to an immovable object with an approved lock, or when kept indoors.
Making a claim (Personal possessions outside the home): Report theft to the police, give the serial number or IMEI and provide proof of purchase.
Home emergency and legal cover: Boiler stopped working in winter and I need an engineer
Home emergency and legal cover: Help with a legal dispute with a neighbour or contractor
Home emergency and legal cover: Optional add-ons for emergency call-outs such as boiler failure and for legal disputes about your home.
Home emergency and legal cover: boiler cover
Home emergency and legal cover: emergency plumber
Home emergency and legal cover: home legal expenses
Home emergency cover (Home emergency and legal cover): Pays for emergency callouts for problems like no heating in winter, a blocked drain or a broken external door.
Legal expenses cover (Home emergency and legal cover): Helps pay legal costs for disputes with contractors, neighbours or tenants, subject to prospects of success.
What is not covered (Home emergency and legal cover): Planned maintenance, routine servicing, and pre-existing faults known before the cover started.
Using the helplines (Home emergency and legal cover): Call the 24-hour numbers on your policy documents with your policy number ready.
Landlord insurance: Insurance for the flat I rent out to tenants
Landlord insurance: Cover if my tenants damage things or stop paying rent
Landlord insurance: Cover for owners who let property, including buildings, contents and loss of rent.
What's covered (Landlord insurance): Buildings, landlord's contents, public liability and optional loss of rent or alternative accommodation for tenants.
Tenants and unoccupied periods (Landlord insurance): Cover is tailored to the type of tenant, and extended empty periods between lets may need to be declared.
Malicious damage by tenants (Landlord insurance): Optional cover pays for damage caused deliberately by tenants, subject to conditions and evidence.
Telling us about changes (Landlord insurance): Tell us if you change tenants, let to students or sublet, as this may affect cover.
Renters' contents insurance: I rent a flat and want protection for my own things
Renters' contents insurance: Covering my belongings and accidental damage to the landlord's furniture
Renters' contents insurance: Cover for tenants for their own belongings and for accidental damage to a landlord's fixtures.
Renters' contents insurance: renting a flat
Renters' contents insurance: contents for tenants
Renters' contents insurance: I spilled or dropped something; knocked something over and broke it
What's covered (Renters' contents insurance): Your own belongings, and optionally accidental damage to the landlord's fixtures and fittings.
What's not covered (Renters' contents insurance): The building itself, which the landlord must insure, and loss of items in shared areas.
Deciding how much cover (Renters' contents insurance): Count the replacement value of everything you own that you would not want to lose.
Moving out (Renters' contents insurance): Cancel or transfer the policy when you leave; tell us your new address in advance.
Single trip cover: Insurance for just one holiday this summer
Single trip cover: Cover for a single break away that I have booked
Single trip cover: Cover for one holiday or journey, from the day you book until you return.
Single trip cover: one-off holiday insurance
Single trip cover: single trip policy
What's covered (Single trip cover): Emergency medical costs, cancellation and curtailment, delayed baggage and personal liability for the dates of your trip.
Start and end dates (Single trip cover): Cover for cancellation starts when you buy the policy; all other sections start on the trip departure date.
Trip length limits (Single trip cover): Single trip policies cover trips up to 31 days in most cases; longer trips may need extended cover.
Buying after you have booked (Single trip cover): Buy as soon as you book to be covered if you must cancel for an insured reason.
Annual multi-trip cover: One policy that covers every holiday and city break I take this year
Annual multi-trip cover: Paying once for all my trips instead of a policy for each
Annual multi-trip cover: Cover for all your trips in a year, with a maximum length for each trip.
Annual multi-trip cover: yearly travel insurance
Annual multi-trip cover: multi trip policy
Annual multi-trip cover: year-round holiday cover
What's covered (Annual multi-trip cover): Every trip you start in the policy year, up to the maximum trip length shown in your schedule, in the countries you selected.
Maximum trip length (Annual multi-trip cover): Typically 31 or 45 days per trip; longer trips need an extension or a separate policy.
Who is on the policy (Annual multi-trip cover): Individual, couple, family and group policies are available, with all travellers named.
Is annual cover worth it (Annual multi-trip cover): It usually pays off from the second trip a year, particularly for European holidays and business trips.
Family and group cover: Covering all the family on the beach holiday
Family and group cover: One policy for the kids and grandparents travelling together
Family and group cover: One travel policy for adults and children on the same trip.
Family and group cover: family travel insurance
Family and group cover: children covered
Who counts as a child (Family and group cover): Children under 18, or under 23 in full-time education, may be included at no extra cost when travelling with an adult.
Group sizes (Family and group cover): Groups of up to ten adults can be covered together provided everyone travels on the same itinerary.
Excess for families (Family and group cover): One excess applies per person per claim; the schedule shows the amounts for each traveller.
Adding a child later (Family and group cover): Contact us to add a new baby or foster child; there may be no additional premium.
Emergency medical cover: I got ill on holiday and ended up in hospital abroad
Emergency medical cover: Paying for treatment and bringing me home if I am hurt overseas
Emergency medical cover: Cover for urgent medical treatment, hospital stays and repatriation if you are ill or injured abroad.
Emergency medical cover: medical expenses abroad
Emergency medical cover: struggling to afford essentials; help buying school uniforms or food; money is tight
What's covered (Emergency medical cover): Hospital treatment, doctor fees, ambulance, and medical repatriation to the UK, up to the medical limit on your policy.
Calling the emergency assistance team (Emergency medical cover): Contact our 24-hour team before incurring large costs or agreeing to treatment, so we can arrange payment directly.
GHIC and EHIC (Emergency medical cover): A UK Global Health Insurance Card gives access to state treatment in the EU but does not cover private care or repatriation.
What's not covered (Emergency medical cover): Treatment that could wait until you return home, and costs of routine or planned procedures.
Pre-existing medical conditions: I have diabetes and need to be sure I can still claim
Pre-existing medical conditions: Telling the insurer about my heart condition before travelling
Pre-existing medical conditions: How to declare an existing health condition so that it is covered.
Pre-existing medical conditions: declare medical conditions
